title: The Waggle Dance of the Honeybee

passage.title: The Waggle Dance of the Honeybee
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
On warm spring mornings, thousands of worker bees leave their wooden hive to search for food. A strong hive needs sweet nectar and yellow pollen from wildflowers to live. Meadows are very wide. A single bee cannot harvest a whole patch of clover alone. Instead, early scouts fly out in every direction to find the best blooms. When a scout spots a thick field of flowers, she drinks a drop of nectar and hurries home to share the news.

Inside the hive, there is no light to show where the flowers grow. The returning scout climbs onto the vertical wax comb in the dark chamber. Other workers gather closely around her and touch her sides with their feelers. The exact location of a distant clover patch, hidden beyond tall pine trees and a winding stream, is clearly shared by the scout bee through a lively figure-eight dance. Scientists call this special movement the waggle dance.

First, the dancer walks in a straight line while shaking her abdomen from side to side. Then she circles back to her starting point from the left and repeats the straight run. Next, she loops back from the right to trace a neat figure eight on the comb. The length of that middle waggle run tells the other bees how far they must fly. A short buzz of one second points to flowers nearby, while a longer run signals a distant meadow.

Telling the distance is only half of the map, so the scout must also show the right direction. She uses the position of the sun in the sky as her compass guide. If the flowers lie straight toward the sun, the scout dances straight up the wax wall. If the patch sits to the right of the sun, she tilts her waggle line to the right by that exact angle. Even on cloudy days, bees can sense sunlight through the mist.

As the dance ends, the scout shares tiny sips of nectar from her stomach with her hive mates. This sample lets the other workers smell the precise type of blossom they should seek once they arrive. Within minutes, dozens of bees launch from the front board and fly straight toward the meadow. By turning simple steps and angles into a living map, honeybees feed their whole colony without speaking a single word.

tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin vertex, meaning 'highest point or top'

tier2Words.definition: the rear section of an insect's body behind the chest and wings
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin abdomen, referring to the lower body cavity
tier2Words.contextClue: The dancer walks in a straight line while shaking the back part of her body from side to side.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"The exact location of a distant clover patch, hidden beyond tall pine trees and a winding stream, is clearly shared by the scout bee through a lively figure-eight dance."

Based on the structure of the sentence, who or what shares the location of the clover patch?

options.text: The tall pine trees and winding stream share the clover patch with the hive.
options.childFeedback: The tall pine trees and winding stream only describe where the distant clover patch is hidden in Paragraph 2—they do not share the news with the hive.

options.text: The scout bee shares the exact location through a figure-eight dance.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'by the scout bee' right after 'is clearly shared' shows that the scout bee is the one sharing the clover patch's location through her dance.

options.text: The distant clover patch performs a lively dance for the scout bee.
options.childFeedback: This flips the action backward! A patch of clover cannot perform a dance; the clover patch's location is the news being shared.

options.text: Scientists inside the dark chamber share the map with the worker bees.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 mentions that scientists named the movement the waggle dance, not that scientists are inside the dark hive sharing a map.

questions.provingSentenceText: The exact location of a distant clover patch, hidden beyond tall pine trees and a winding stream, is clearly shared by the scout bee through a lively figure-eight dance.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'by the scout bee' right after 'is clearly shared' shows that the scout bee is the one sharing the clover patch's location through her dance.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive-voice sentence, 'The exact location of a distant clover patch' receives the action, while 'by the scout bee' names the actor performing the sharing.
questions.retryHint: Look for the 'by' phrase right after 'is clearly shared' in Paragraph 2 to see who performs the action.

questions.prompt:
Read these sentences from Paragraph 5:

"As the dance ends, the scout shares tiny sips of nectar from her stomach with her hive mates. This sample lets the other workers smell the precise type of blossom they should seek once they arrive."

What does the word precise mean as it is used in Paragraph 5?

options.text: Careless and random
options.childFeedback: If the flower scent were careless and random, the worker bees would not know which blossoms to search for when they reach the meadow.

options.text: Wilted and dried out
options.childFeedback: The scout bee just drank fresh sweet nectar from blooming flowers, so the blossoms in Paragraph 5 are not wilted and dried out.

options.text: Hidden in the dark
options.childFeedback: Although the bees are inside the dark hive during the dance, 'precise' describes the specific type of blossom they smell in the nectar sample.

options.text: Exact and specific
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 5, 'precise' means exact and specific, because smelling the nectar sample tells the worker bees the exact kind of flower to look for in the meadow.

questions.provingSentenceText: This sample lets the other workers smell the precise type of blossom they should seek once they arrive.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 5, 'precise' means exact and specific, because smelling the nectar sample tells the worker bees the exact kind of flower to look for in the meadow.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 5, smelling the nectar sample tells the worker bees the exact, specific ('precise') kind of flower to look for in the meadow.
questions.retryHint: Think about how smelling a tiny sip of nectar helps the bees know which type of flower to find in Paragraph 5.

questions.prompt: According to Paragraph 3, how does a scout bee show other bees how far away the flowers are?

options.text: By changing how long she performs the middle waggle run of her dance
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 explains that the length of the middle waggle run shows the distance: a short one-second buzz means flowers are nearby, while a longer run means a distant meadow.

options.text: By tapping her feelers against the wax comb once for every mile
options.childFeedback: Other workers touch the scout's sides with their feelers in Paragraph 2, but the scout never taps the wax comb once per mile.

options.text: By flying in tall circles above the roof of the wooden hive
options.childFeedback: The scout performs her figure-eight dance on the vertical wax comb inside the dark hive, not by flying in circles above the roof.

options.text: By dropping yellow pollen grains in a long trail across the floor
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 describes the scout tracing a figure eight on the comb and shaking her abdomen, not dropping a trail of pollen across the floor.

questions.provingSentenceText: The length of that middle waggle run tells the other bees how far they must fly.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 3 explains that the length of the middle waggle run shows the distance: a short one-second buzz means flowers are nearby, while a longer run means a distant meadow.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 states that the duration/length of the middle waggle run communicates the distance to the flowers (a short run means nearby, while a longer run means farther away).
questions.retryHint: Check the last two sentences of Paragraph 3 to see what a short buzz versus a longer waggle run tells the other bees.

questions.prompt: How do Paragraphs 3 and 4 work together to help the reader understand the waggle dance?

options.text: Paragraph 3 tells how bees make wax combs, and Paragraph 4 tells how bees store honey for winter.
options.childFeedback: Neither paragraph explains how bees build wax combs or store winter honey; both paragraphs focus on how the waggle dance guides bees to flowers.

options.text: Paragraph 3 describes a problem inside the hive, and Paragraph 4 explains how beekeepers fix it.
options.childFeedback: Beekeepers are never mentioned in Paragraphs 3 or 4; the scout bees solve the challenge of sharing flower locations all on their own.

options.text: Paragraph 3 explains how the dance shows distance, and Paragraph 4 explains how the dance shows direction.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 explains how the length of the waggle run tells the distance, and Paragraph 4 explains how the angle of the dance uses the sun to show the right direction.

options.text: Paragraph 3 argues that bees cannot see in the dark, and Paragraph 4 proves that bees never fly on cloudy days.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 actually states the exact opposite about cloudy weather: even on cloudy days, bees can still sense sunlight through the mist.

questions.provingSentenceText: Telling the distance is only half of the map, so the scout must also show the right direction.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 3 explains how the length of the waggle run tells the distance, and Paragraph 4 explains how the angle of the dance uses the sun to show the right direction.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 details how the waggle run's length communicates distance, and Paragraph 4 transitions ('Telling the distance is only half of the map...') to explain how the angle of the dance relative to gravity shows the sun's direction.
questions.retryHint: Read the first sentence of Paragraph 4 to see how it connects the distance from Paragraph 3 with the second half of the bee's map.

questions.prompt: Part A: Which statement best summarizes the main idea of the entire passage?

options.text: Honeybees cannot find clover patches whenever clouds block the bright spring sun.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 says bees can still sense sunlight through the mist on cloudy days, so clouds do not stop them from finding clover.

options.text: Wax combs inside a wooden hive must always be built near a winding stream and tall pine trees.
options.childFeedback: The pine trees and winding stream in Paragraph 2 only describe where one distant clover patch is located, not a rule for where hives must be built.

options.text: A single worker bee can easily gather enough pollen from a meadow to feed the whole colony.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 says the exact opposite: a single bee cannot harvest a whole patch of clover alone, which is why scouts must guide other workers.

options.text: Scout honeybees use a detailed dance and nectar samples to guide hive mates to distant flowers.
options.childFeedback: The whole passage explains how scout honeybees find flowers and use the waggle dance plus tiny sips of nectar to guide the rest of the hive to food.

questions.provingSentenceText: By turning simple steps and angles into a living map, honeybees feed their whole colony without speaking a single word.
questions.childTip: The whole passage explains how scout honeybees find flowers and use the waggle dance plus tiny sips of nectar to guide the rest of the hive to food.
questions.parentExplanation: The passage as a whole explains how scout bees communicate distance, direction, and flower scent through the waggle dance and nectar samples so the colony can harvest food.
questions.retryHint: Look for the choice that covers the main point of the whole passage: how scout bees guide their hive mates to flowers.

questions.prompt: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "A single bee cannot harvest a whole patch of clover alone."
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 1 only explains why one bee needs help, without mentioning the waggle dance or nectar samples that guide the hive.

options.text: "By turning simple steps and angles into a living map, honeybees feed their whole colony without speaking a single word."
options.childFeedback: This final sentence from Paragraph 5 sums up the main idea from Question 5 by showing how the dance's steps and angles create a living map that feeds the whole colony.

options.text: "Even on cloudy days, bees can sense sunlight through the mist."
options.childFeedback: This detail from Paragraph 4 only explains how bees handle cloudy weather, rather than summarizing how the dance guides the whole colony to food.

options.text: "Inside the hive, there is no light to show where the flowers grow."
options.childFeedback: This detail from Paragraph 2 only describes the dark inside of the hive, without explaining how the scout bee shares her map with the other workers.

questions.childTip: This final sentence from Paragraph 5 sums up the main idea from Question 5 by showing how the dance's steps and angles create a living map that feeds the whole colony.
